newsitem.title: GERMANY: BMW profit rise gathers pace in first half.
newsitem.headline: BMW profit rise gathers pace in first half.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG reported on Tuesday a robust 30 percent increase in net profit during the first half of 1997 as new models and a strong dollar boosted results.

BMW, which reported an 18.5 percent rise in 1996 profits, said net profit climbed 100 million marks in the first six months of 1997 to 435 million marks on sales growth of 15.5 percent to 29.10 billion marks.
The carmaker, which is known for offering conservative forecasts, added it expected sales and profit to climb for the year as a whole but did not specify by how much.

Analysts said the results reflected the strength of the dollar and a low base figure due to a model changeover as much as the undeniable success of new models like the 5-Series executive class saloon and the Z3 roadster sports car.

"The figures are a bit better than expected, but generally in line with our forecasts," said Stephen Reitman, analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. "We should see profits up by about one third for the year as a whole."

Deliveries of BMW branded cars climbed to 350,788 vehicles from 318,625 in the year-ago period. Deliveries of cars made by Britain's Rover Group, which BMW bought in 1994, climbed to 250,382 vehicles from 238,154.
Analysts said the first-half figures reinforced their belief that BMW will report group net profit of around one billion marks for the year as a whole -- compared with 820 million in 1996.

Investors intially cheered the results, pushing BMW's share price up 12.50 marks to 1,482.50 marks while the 30-share DAX index was moving the opposite way. But BMW shares were unable to hold the gains and fell into negative territory.

Although BMW branded cars made a strong advance in the U.S., where deliveries climbed 25 percent to 62,000 units, the most statisfying story for the first half may be BMW's success in its home market.
BMW, which faces a tough battle with Audi AG, said its share of the German car market climbed to 6.5 percent in the first half from 6.1 percent in first half 1996.

With the 5-Series giving it an edge in the market share battle, BMW has kept demand for its long-serving 3-Series alive with no fewer than eight variations including compact, cabriolet and estate versions, one analyst said.
The solid jump in profit was due to a trio of factors -- the dollar's climb against the mark, a low base figure and good demand for BMW branded cars, analysts said.
Indeed, the dollar has climbed roughly 20 percent against the mark so far this year, boosting sales and profits by increasing the value of business conducted in the U.S.
Sabine Bluemel, analyst at IMI Sigeco in London, warned against exaggerating the impact of the dollar's climb, saying that BMW was hedged against foreign exchange swings.
The first half of 1996 was unusally difficult for BMW as it updated its 5-Series model, leading consumers to hold off purchases of the previous executive class car.
Finally, analysts said BMW has built on its reputation for high-quality, sporty cars with models such the Z3 roadster selling as fast as BMW can make them.
"BMW is upbeat about its prospects, driven by the high-margin 5-Series," Bluemel said.

The biggest question marks hanging over BMW are the future of money-losing Rover, which chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder promises will be in the black by 2000, and the new 3-Series model which analysts expect to be released early next year.

Many, however, see Rover on a solid recovery course with Land Rover sport utility vehicles selling well and BMW taking no chances with the new 3-Series, designing a model which analysts said maintains a close styling link with the existing model and the 5-Series.
